content.title: About
content.content: Blueberries are small, dark‑blue berries of the Vaccinium corymbosum shrub, native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. The berries are sweet‑tart, fragrant, and have a soft, juicy texture. Blueberries are eaten fresh, used in baked goods, desserts, smoothies, and jams.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Blueberries belong to the cranberry family and are closely related to bilberries and lingonberries.
Anthocyanins give the berries their deep blue color and provide strong antioxidant activity.
Wild blueberries are often sweeter than cultivated varieties.
Native American tribes have used blueberries traditionally to support eye health.
The harvest season typically runs from July through September.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Blueberries contain anthocyanins and vitamin C, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports vision
items.content: Flavonoids in blueberries may improve night vision and reduce age‑related eye decline.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low‑calorie snack
items.content: Blueberries are low in calories, making them suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The berries supply vitamin K, vitamin E, manganese, and iron, important for metabolic processes.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to blueberries.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Non‑organic berries can contain pesticide residues; thorough washing is recommended.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Large portions may raise blood sugar levels in people with diabetes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Blueberries can be eaten fresh, added to yogurt, oatmeal, baked goods, smoothies, or cooked into sauces and jams. Freezing preserves their flavor and nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store blueberries in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 7 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a single layer on a tray, then transfer to a freezer bag.

chicken-ns-as-to-part-baked-coated-skin-.title: Chicken, NS as part, baked, coated, skin/coating not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide. This entry refers to a baked chicken portion that is coated, with the skin or coating not intended to be eaten because it may contain excess fat and additives.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken meat is rich in high‑quality protein that is easily digested.
Baking retains most nutrients compared with deep‑frying.
Coatings can be made from whole grains, breadcrumbs, or spices, giving a crunchy crust.
Chicken is a good source of B‑vitamins, especially niacin (B3) and pyridoxine (B6).
Various cultures serve baked chicken with different sauces and side dishes.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Protein supports tissue growth, repair, and a healthy immune system.

items.title: Low carbohydrate level
items.content: Makes it suitable for low‑carb diets and blood‑sugar control.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Help convert food into energy and support nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals: phosphorus and selenium
items.content: Phosphorus is important for bone health, while selenium provides antioxidant benefits.

items.title: Low fat when skin is removed
items.content: Removing the skin reduces saturated fat, benefiting cardiovascular health.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Sodium in the coating
items.content: Prepared coatings often contain salt; choose low‑sodium options if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Trans fats in processed coatings
items.content: Some commercial breadings may contain partially hydrogenated oils, which should be limited.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the baked chicken without skin and add it to salads, sandwiches, or use as a filling for tacos. The coating can be eaten separately if it does not contain undesirable additives.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked chicken in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before serving.

frozen-mocha-coffee-drink-decaffeinated-.title: Frozen Decaf Mocha Coffee Drink with Non‑Dairy Milk and Whipped Cream

content.title: About
content.content: Frozen decaf mocha coffee is a refreshing beverage made from cold‑brewed coffee flavored with chocolate, blended with non‑dairy milk (soy, almond, or oat) and topped with a light layer of non‑dairy whipped cream. The drink contains no caffeine, making it suitable for those who want the coffee taste without stimulation.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Frozen coffee drinks first appeared in the United States in the early 1990s as an alternative to traditional ice cream.
Decaffeinated coffee is produced either by extracting caffeine from regular beans or by using beans that are naturally low in caffeine.
The chocolate flavor in mocha coffee is often enhanced with real cocoa mass or natural cocoa syrup.
Non‑dairy milks give the drink a unique texture and make it vegan‑friendly and suitable for lactose‑intolerant consumers.
Non‑dairy whipped cream is usually made from coconut cream or soy‑based “whipping” products.

items.title: Low caffeine content
items.content: The absence of caffeine makes the drink safe for children, pregnant women, and people sensitive to stimulants.

items.title: Antioxidants from cocoa
items.content: Cocoa is rich in flavonoids, which may support cardiovascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins from coffee
items.content: Even decaffeinated coffee retains small amounts of B2 and B3 vitamins that aid metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D from fortified plant milk
items.content: Fortified non‑dairy milks often contain calcium and vitamin D, beneficial for bone health.

items.title: Probiotics in some plant milks
items.content: When fermented oat or soy milk is used, the drink can provide beneficial bacteria.

items.title: Allergy to plant ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to soy, almond, or oat milk.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweeteners such as sugar or syrup are often added, increasing the drink’s calorie count.

items.title: Caloric whipped cream
items.content: Non‑dairy whipped cream made from coconut cream is high in saturated fat.

items.title: Additive presence
items.content: Certain versions may contain artificial flavors or stabilizers, which some consumers prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the frozen mocha coffee in a tall glass with a straw, enjoying its cold, creamy texture. Optional toppings include fresh berries, a dusting of cinnamon, or cocoa powder. The drink can be stored in the freezer and thawed for 5‑10 minutes before serving to retain its smooth consistency.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen mocha coffee in an airtight container at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After three months, the texture and flavor may begin to degrade. Before consumption, allow the drink to soften slightly but not fully melt to preserve its creamy mouthfeel.

content.title: About
content.content: Pork sausage, reduced fat (991) is a cooked‑smoked product made from lean pork meat, low‑fat cuts and a modest blend of spices. Part of the fat is mechanically removed and water is added, lowering the calorie count and saturated‑fat content while preserving the classic pork sausage flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fat reduction is achieved by mechanical trimming and water addition, which keeps the product juicy.
In Russia these sausages are often used in diet menus and institutional catering where a balanced protein‑fat ratio is required.
Traditional recipes include garlic, black pepper and paprika, but reduced‑fat versions often cut back on salt.
Reduced‑fat sausage loses aroma faster during prolonged storage, so it should be consumed within 5‑7 days after opening.
In some countries (e.g., Germany) similar products are called “Magerwurst” and are popular among athletes.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 18 g of high‑quality animal protein, essential for muscle repair and immune function.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Reduced saturated fat helps maintain healthy blood cholesterol levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, which support energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides iron, zinc and selenium – important micronutrients for blood formation and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Lower calorie content compared with regular sausage
items.content: The reduced‑fat formulation brings the energy value down to roughly 150 kcal per 100 g, making it more suitable for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Like most smoked meat products, the sausage is high in salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pork proteins.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Nitrites and other preservatives may be added for shelf life; sensitive people should limit intake.

items.title: Heat treatment
items.content: Insufficiently heated sausage may harbor pathogenic bacteria; it should be warmed to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sausage can be eaten cold as sliced meat, added to sandwiches, salads, omelets, or used in hot dishes such as stews and casseroles. Lightly pan‑frying enhances its aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container. After opening, consume within 5‑7 days. For longer storage, freeze up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: A salami sandwich on white bread is a classic snack consisting of sliced salami placed between two pieces of soft white bread. The sandwich offers the aromatic, slightly spicy flavor of salami combined with the gentle texture of the bread, making it a popular quick bite.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Salami originates from Italy, traditionally made from pork, beef and a blend of spices.
White bread is often used because its neutral taste does not overpower the flavor of the sausage.
Salami sandwiches are commonly served in cafés and snack bars as a fast lunch or snack.
Salami can be mild or hot depending on the spices added.
In many countries the sandwich is enhanced with cheese, mustard or pickled vegetables.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Salami provides a substantial amount of protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Meat products like salami are good sources of heme iron, which supports oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 present in salami is important for nervous system health and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The sandwich delivers quick calories, convenient for an active lifestyle.

items.title: Provides zinc
items.content: Zinc in salami supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Salami is typically high in salt, which can raise blood pressure if consumed frequently.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Processed meats are rich in saturated fats, which in excess may contribute to cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Preservatives and nitrites
items.content: Some salami varieties contain nitrites, which can be harmful with long‑term high intake.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to certain meats or spices may experience reactions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The sandwich can be calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable, especially on a diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is ready to eat straight after assembly. It can be halved, topped with mustard, mayo, cheese or fresh vegetables to taste. For a softer bread texture, the slices are sometimes lightly toasted.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the assembled sandwich in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Keep salami separately, wrapped in plastic film, to preserve its flavor.

content.title: About
content.content: Wheat (Triticum aestivum and related species) is a cereal grain grown around the world and one of the most important staple foods. Its kernels are eaten whole as wheat berries, cracked as bulgur, and ground into flour for bread, pasta, noodles, couscous, and baked goods. Wheat has a mild, nutty flavor and contains gluten, a protein that gives dough its elasticity.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wheat was first domesticated about 10,000 years ago in the Fertile Crescent of the Middle East.
A wheat kernel has three parts: the bran, the germ, and the endosperm, and whole wheat contains all three.
Durum wheat is used for pasta, while softer wheats are used for bread and pastries.
Bulgur, couscous, semolina, and farro are all made from wheat.
Wheat is one of the most widely grown crops in the world.

items.title: Source of energy
items.content: Wheat is rich in carbohydrates, which provide energy.

items.title: Whole wheat provides dietary fiber
items.content: The bran in whole wheat provides fiber that supports digestion and fullness.

items.title: Provides B vitamins
items.content: Wheat contains thiamin, niacin, and folate, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Wheat contains manganese, selenium, magnesium, and phosphorus.

items.title: Provides plant protein
items.content: Wheat provides protein, although it is lower in the amino acid lysine.

items.title: Celiac disease and gluten sensitivity
items.content: Wheat contains gluten and must be avoided by people with celiac disease and by people with non-celiac gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: Wheat is one of the more common food allergens, and wheat allergy can be serious, especially in children.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Wheat contains fructans that may cause gas or bloating in people with irritable bowel syndrome.

items.title: Refined products and mold
items.content: Refined wheat products have less fiber than whole grains, and wheat stored in damp conditions can develop mold.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Whole wheat berries can be soaked and simmered until chewy for salads, soups, and pilafs. Bulgur and couscous cook quickly and make good side dishes, and wheat flour is used in bread, flatbreads, pasta, pancakes, and baking. Choose whole wheat products for more fiber.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store wheat berries, bulgur, and flour in airtight containers in a cool, dry place. Whole wheat flour keeps for a shorter time than white flour because of the germ's oils, so refrigerate or freeze it for longer storage. Cooked wheat should be refrigerated and eaten within three to five days.
